title: The robber who became a poet
hookLine: a highway robber becomes a poet; the Gita says the door was never locked
carry: bhakti is open to anyone who turns

lines: WILL YOUR FAMILY SHARE THE WRONG?
cards: Valmiki, the poet of the Ramayana, was once a highway robber, or so the story people tell goes, stopping travelers in the forest.
One day he stopped a sage, who asked him a simple question: your family shares what you steal, but will they share the wrongs you did to get it? The robber went home and asked. They said no.
He came back shaken, and the sage gave him the name of Rama to repeat. He sat repeating it so long that an anthill grew over him. And he came out a poet.

teach.b: Verse twenty-nine: I am the same to all beings. No one is hateful to me, and no one is my favorite. But those who worship me with love are in me, and I am in them.

teach.h: EVEN THE WORST, TURNED, IS GOOD.
teach.b: Then verse thirty, the one that surprises people: even if someone of very bad conduct worships me with undivided devotion, they should be considered good, because they've made the right resolve. Not good eventually.
Good now, because of which way they've turned. Verse thirty-one: quickly they become righteous and reach lasting peace.
And Krishna tells Arjuna to announce it: my devotee never perishes. Na me bhaktah pranashyati.

teach.h: A WIDER CIRCLE, READ TWO WAYS.
teach.b: Verse thirty-two widens the circle. Those who take refuge in me, even those the society of the time held low, women, merchants and farmers, laborers, reach the highest goal.
The verse names groups the ranking of its day placed below others, and readers today argue about its wording; some find it painful, some read it as those groups being singled out for welcome.

Some hear a widening: doors that were closed, pushed open. Verse thirty-four, the chapter's last, is the whole of it in a line: fix your mind on me, be devoted to me, offer to me, bow to me, and you'll come to me.
In the Gita's telling, nobody is too far gone to turn.

how: Many Hindus hold that devotion to God is open to everyone regardless of birth or past, and the story of Valmiki, the robber who became the poet of the Ramayana, is widely told to show that anyone can turn.

o: a devotee, one who loves God
a priest who leads temple rites
a saint free of all wrongdoing

games.q: what's inside the verses — tap the pairs.
p: even the worst, turned, is good
the robber who became a poet

s: the Gita says some people are too bad to turn to God
verse 30: even one of very bad conduct, turned with undivided devotion, is to be counted good.
Krishna tells Arjuna to declare it: my devotee never perishes
no one is hateful and no one is a favorite; those who love are in him, and he in them.

games.q: someone with a terrible past turns to God with their whole heart. how does verse 30 say they should be regarded?
o: with suspicion, until they prove themselves.
as good, because they've made the right resolve.
as good only after many lifetimes.
games.why: as good, now: sadhur eva sa mantavyah. verse 31 adds that they quickly become righteous and reach lasting peace.

practice: Think of someone you've written off: someone who hurt you, a public figure, maybe a younger version of yourself.

You don't have to excuse anything they did; just hold them for a moment in the light of verse thirty, that turning is always possible. Breathe in and picture the door open; breathe out and let a little of the hardness go.

wordCard.voice: Bhakta. Devotee, one who loves God. Gita nine, thirty: whoever turns with undivided devotion, whatever they've done, is to be counted good. No one is outside.

orig.note: Sanskrit: bhakta, devotee, one who loves God; from bhaj, to share in, to worship.

carryVoice: Your line: bhakti is open to anyone who turns. The door stays open, whatever's behind you. Chapter nine, complete.

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 9.29–9.31 (even the worst; my devotee never perishes)
the Valmiki conversion story (later tradition, e.g. the Adhyatma Ramayana and popular retellings)
